title: AI Coding Agents in 2026: How Codex, Jules, Devin, OpenHands and Claude Code Differ
description: A practical comparison of the coding agents developers actually use in 2026 — asynchronous cloud agents, terminal agents and IDE agents — and how to choose between them.
author: Use AI Tools
content:
# AI Coding Agents in 2026: How Codex, Jules, Devin, OpenHands and Claude Code Differ

"Coding agent" now covers three different products, and most disappointment comes from buying one kind while expecting another. The categories are asynchronous cloud agents, terminal agents and IDE agents. They solve different problems and they fail differently.

## 1. Asynchronous cloud agents

You hand over a task, walk away, and come back to a pull request.

**[[link:/tool/jules|Jules]]** is Google's version. You point it at a GitHub repository or label an issue, and it clones the repo into a cloud VM, plans the change, produces a diff and opens a pull request for review. Plans are tiered by daily tasks and concurrency, with the higher tiers using newer Gemini models. The design assumption is that you will review, not watch.

**[[link:/tool/openai-codex|OpenAI Codex]]** works similarly, as a cloud agent that can run several tasks in parallel, and also as a CLI in your own terminal. The parallel-task model suits maintenance work: five dependency bumps at once rather than one.

**[[link:/tool/devin|Devin]]** from Cognition is the original "autonomous software engineer" framing, and now also backs a desktop product. One observable signal of consolidation: the Windsurf domain now redirects to Devin, which tells you how much of this category is converging on agents rather than editors.

Where they fail: anything requiring unwritten context. If the reason a function is shaped that way lives in someone's head, an async agent will produce a confident, wrong diff.

## 2. Terminal and local agents

You stay in the loop, but the agent runs commands.

**[[link:/tool/openhands|OpenHands]]** is the open-source platform for this: it edits files, runs commands, browses and opens pull requests, and you can run it locally, in CI or hosted. This is the option when the code cannot leave your network or when you want to inspect exactly what the agent is allowed to do.

**[[link:/tool/claude-code|Claude Code]]** runs in the terminal with the repository as context, and is the common choice for refactors where you want to steer each step.

**[[link:/tool/continuedev|Continue.dev]]** is open source and spans VS Code, JetBrains and the terminal, with bring-your-own-model support and team configuration shared through a hub. If you already run your own model endpoint, this is where that pays off.

Where they fail: long unattended runs. The value here is steering, so treat them as a power tool, not a worker.

## 3. IDE agents for large codebases

**[[link:/tool/augment-code|Augment Code]]** is built around a context engine that indexes millions of lines, so multi-file edits and pull-request review stay workable once a repository exceeds a single context window.

**[[link:/tool/trae|Trae]]** is ByteDance's AI-native IDE, with a builder mode that plans multi-file features and an agent for terminal and debugging tasks, and free access to mainstream models.

**[[link:/tool/cursor|Cursor]]** and [[link:/tool/github-copilot|GitHub Copilot]] remain the default choices for everyday editing, and both have moved into agent mode rather than pure autocomplete.

Where they fail: they inherit your editor's blind spots. If the index is stale, suggestions are confidently wrong.

## 4. App builders, a different job

**[[link:/tool/boltnew|Bolt.new]]** generates, runs and deploys a full-stack app from a prompt inside the browser. **[[link:/tool/lovable|Lovable]]** does similar work with code you can export. These are excellent for prototypes and awkward for large existing systems — judge them as scaffolding, not as a development process.

## How to choose

Ask one question: do you want to review the result, or steer the work?

- **Review the result, task is well defined** → asynchronous agent. [[link:/tool/jules|Jules]] for GitHub-hosted work with PR review; [[link:/tool/openai-codex|OpenAI Codex]] if you want several tasks moving at once.
- **Steer the work, code is sensitive** → local agent. [[link:/tool/openhands|OpenHands]] for full control and self-hosting, [[link:/tool/claude-code|Claude Code]] for terminal refactors, [[link:/tool/continuedev|Continue.dev]] if you bring your own model.
- **Working in a large existing repository** → an IDE agent with real indexing, such as [[link:/tool/augment-code|Augment Code]], or the agent mode of the editor your team already uses.
- **Prototype to show someone** → [[link:/tool/boltnew|Bolt.new]] or [[link:/tool/lovable|Lovable]].

## What to put in place first

Agents are only as good as what they can verify. Three things make a measurable difference:

1. **Tests with real coverage.** An async agent without tests produces plausible diffs you cannot trust.
2. **A documented build and lint command.** Agents that can run your checks catch their own mistakes.
3. **Repository instructions.** A short file describing conventions, structure and what not to touch is the cheapest accuracy improvement available.

Start with low-stakes tasks — dependency bumps, missing tests, a documented bug — and let the agent earn scope.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between an AI coding agent and a code assistant?

acceptedAnswer.text: An assistant suggests code as you type. An agent plans and executes a task: it reads the repository, edits files, runs commands and returns a diff or a pull request. Tools like Jules and OpenAI Codex work asynchronously, while Claude Code and OpenHands stay under your control in the terminal.

mainEntity.name: Can I self-host an AI coding agent?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. OpenHands is open source and can run locally, in CI or self-hosted, which is the standard choice when code cannot leave your network. Continue also supports bring-your-own-model setups for IDE and terminal work.

mainEntity.name: Are AI coding agents reliable enough for production code?

acceptedAnswer.text: They are reliable for well-scoped tasks with test coverage: dependency bumps, missing tests, documented bugs and mechanical refactors. They are unreliable where the requirement depends on context that is not written down. Reviewing the diff remains mandatory.
